new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first vowel (first syllable) of the word. In compounds, primary stress may instead fall on the first vowel of the last stem, depending on grammatical structure (kin term + personal name combinations pattern like compounds, with primary stress on the second element). Full vowel quality/length contrasts exist only in stressed syllables; non-initial unstressed vowels are reduced to schwa / syllabic consonants (analysed as unstressed /a/).
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'Secondary stress falls on the other vowels in a predictable way' (i.e. on non-initial full vowels of the chart, as opposed to reduced unstressed /a/); no rhythmic/positional algorithm is given. Orthographically, a non-initial /a/ that bears secondary stress is marked with a grave accent (p.238, p.240: /ngathàna/ [ŋatàn(a)] vs /puthana/ [putən(a)]), and non-initial stems of compounds carry secondary stress, signalled by the hyphen (/ma'a-ngamala/).
new_statements.exceptions: Hedges 'usually predictable', 'In general'. Stated departures: compounds, where primary stress 'may fall on the first vowel of the last stem... depending on its grammatical structure' (p.235); kin term + personal name: 'Such combinations bear a strong resemblance to compounds, and primary stress is borne by the second element (the name). The same pattern obtains with terms such as /piip-thawana/ (FB-) or /piinhiy-kenycha/ (WM)' (p.211). Sutton & Hale 2021 p.182 fn.5 restates: stressed /e/ 'may also appear in the first syllable of the second part of a compound'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement ('first vowel of any word'; 2021 fn.5 'primary word stress'). Phrase stress is mentioned separately (p.241: laminal assimilation direction 'may be governed by phrase stress (in both cases primary stress is on the verb...)'). Citation forms are given in underlying shape with final /a/ (p.240), which surfaces as [a]/schwa/zero depending on intonation-contour terminals (p.239). Scope (p.234): Wik-Ngathana of the Wolmby/Peemuggina family at Cape Keerweer; 'Most of it would also be an accurate description of the Wik-Ngathana of the Kendall River Woollas and of the Wik-Iinychanya', and structurally of Wik-Ngatharra.
new_statements.identity_note: Sutton 1978 Appendix 1 describes exactly this languoid: the Wik-Ngathana (later spelled Wik-Ngathan) of the Wolmby/Peemuggina family, Cape Keerweer (wikn1245, ISO wig, Austlang Y54). Sutton adds that it is also accurate for Kendall River Wik-Ngathana and for Wik-Iinychanya (with some lexical/phonological differences), and 'at the structural level' for Wik-Ngatharra (= Wik-Alken/Wikalkan, wika1238). Note: the catalog's existing wika1238 entry  was coded from this same Wik-Ngathana description plus the 2021 footnote, so wikn1245 is the primary object of the source and wika1238 the extension; the two entries share one source but are distinct Glottolog languages, not duplicates.

sources.citation: Sutton, Peter & Ken Hale. 2021. Linguistic Organisation and Native Title: The Wik Case, Australia. Canberra: ANU Press (Asia-Pacific Linguistics). doi:10.22459/LONT.2021.
sources.note: p.xv: schwa written /e/ following Sutton (1995a). p.181 (Hale, ch.7): Wik-Ngathan among Wik languages that reduced 'unstressed post-consonantal vowels'; free pronouns stressed, dependent pronouns atonic (Wik-Me'nh/Wik-Mungkan). p.182 fn.5 (Sutton): 'for Wik-Ngathan and Wik-Ngatharr... there is also a phoneme /e/ that occurs in the first syllable of a word. That is the vowel with primary word stress. It may also appear in the first syllable of the second part of a compound.' p.60 fn.31: 'Wik-Way... based on primary word stress on /wik/'. Orthographic footnotes, consistent with 1978.
'wig Wik-Ngathana' occurs only in the ISO code table; no StressTyp2 lect/entry for this language.
